topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: An owner who lives in one unit of a building containing four or fewer total dwelling units, and who rents out the other units without using a real estate broker or discriminatory advertising, may claim an exemption from many Fair Housing Act provisions commonly known as the:
choice_a: 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption for small owner-occupied buildings under 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b)
choice_b: Housing for Older Persons Act exemption
explanation: 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b) exempts rooms or units in dwellings containing living quarters occupied by no more than four families living independently, if the owner actually maintains and occupies one of those units as a residence -- commonly called the small owner-occupied building or 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption. Even an exempt owner remains bound by the Act's separate prohibition on discriminatory advertising.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Under 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b), a private individual who personally sells a single-family home without using a real estate broker or agent, and without publishing discriminatory advertising, may claim an exemption from Fair Housing Act coverage, but only if that individual:
choice_a: Does not own an interest in more than three such single-family homes at any one time
choice_b: Owns an unlimited number of single-family rental homes
choice_c: Uses a licensed real estate broker to market the property
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's single-family-home exemption under Section 3603(b) is limited to owners of no more than three such homes at a time who sell or rent without a broker's involvement and without discriminatory advertising -- a narrower exemption than many licensees assume.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3603(b)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A religious organization may limit the sale, rental, or occupancy of dwellings it owns or operates for a non-commercial purpose to members of its own religion under the Fair Housing Act's exemption in 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(a), provided that:
choice_a: Membership in the religion itself is not restricted on account of race, color, or national origin
choice_b: The organization may also freely restrict membership by race without limitation
choice_c: The dwellings must be open to the general public
choice_d: No such exemption exists under federal law
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's religious organization exemption allows preference for co-religionists in housing the organization owns or operates for non-commercial purposes, but only if the religion's own membership is not itself restricted based on race, color, or national origin.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(a)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A bona fide private club that is not in fact open to the public may limit the rental or occupancy of lodgings it owns or operates for other than a commercial purpose to its own members under the Fair Housing Act, as long as the lodging is provided:
choice_a: As an incident to the club's primary purpose, and not as a pretext for otherwise-prohibited discrimination
choice_b: To any member of the general public who pays a fee
choice_c: Only after obtaining HUD pre-approval for each unit rented
choice_d: In a building of five or more units, since smaller buildings never qualify
explanation: The Fair Housing Act's private club exemption is narrow: it applies only to lodgings genuinely incidental to a private club's primary (non-housing) purpose and not open to the public, preventing the exemption from becoming a loophole for organized discrimination.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(a)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: For housing to qualify for the Fair Housing Act's '55 or older' housing exemption from familial-status protections, federal law requires, among other conditions, that:
choice_a: At least 80 percent of the occupied units have at least one occupant age 55 or older, combined with published policies and procedures demonstrating an intent to operate as 55-or-older housing
choice_b: 100 percent of units be occupied exclusively by persons over age 70
choice_c: No age-verification procedures of any kind are required
choice_d: The community remain open to families with minor children without any restriction
explanation: The Housing for Older Persons Act's '55 or older' exemption requires at least 80% of occupied units to have a resident 55+, published policies demonstrating that intent, and compliance with age-verification procedures -- a more demanding, multi-part test than the simpler '62 or older' category.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions -- Housing for Older Persons Act), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(b)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A retirement community that is intended for, and solely occupied by, persons age 62 or older qualifies for the Fair Housing Act's Housing for Older Persons Act exemption without needing to separately satisfy the:
choice_a: 80-percent-occupancy and published-policy requirements that apply specifically to the separate '55 or older' housing category
choice_b: Fair Housing Act at all, since '62 or older' communities are entirely unregulated by any law
choice_c: Building codes of the state in which the community is located
choice_d: Requirement that residents pay any form of rent or fee
explanation: The '62 or older' HOPA category is narrower but simpler than the '55 or older' category -- it requires the housing to be intended for, and solely occupied by, persons 62 and older, without the 80%-occupancy and published-policy conditions that apply to the '55 or older' exemption.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 (fair housing exemptions -- Housing for Older Persons Act), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Section 3607(b)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: An owner who otherwise qualifies for a Fair Housing Act exemption, such as the small owner-occupied building exemption, nonetheless remains fully subject to which prohibition?
choice_a: The Act's prohibition on discriminatory advertising under 42 U.S.C. Section 3604(c), which no exemption excuses
choice_b: Nothing at all -- exempt owners are excused from every Fair Housing Act provision without limitation
choice_c: Only state real estate licensing requirements, and nothing federal
explanation: Even the Fair Housing Act's owner exemptions expressly do not permit the publication of any discriminatory advertisement or notice in violation of Section 3604(c) -- the advertising prohibition applies universally regardless of an owner's exempt status.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3 and V.C.5 (fair housing exemptions and prohibited advertising), Pearson VUE #094401; 42 U.S.C. Sections 3603(b), 3604(c)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Compared with the seven protected classes enumerated under the federal Fair Housing Act, the classes explicitly listed in Texas Property Code Section 301.021 (the Texas Fair Housing Act) are:
choice_a: Race, color, religion, sex, familial status, and national origin -- with disability addressed separately in Section 301.025 -- meaning Texas does not add any protected class beyond the federal list
choice_b: An entirely separate list that adds sexual orientation and source of income as Texas-specific protected classes
choice_c: Only race and color, omitting the other federal classes
choice_d: A list that excludes familial status entirely
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 301.021 tracks six of the federal Fair Housing Act's classes directly, with disability discrimination addressed in the separate Section 301.025 -- together mirroring, not expanding, the federal seven-class framework rather than adding state-specific protected classes.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 301 (Texas Fair Housing Act), Sections 301.021, 301.025, verified via texas.public.law; Pearson VUE #094400 Texas Broker State Law Content Outline

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Under Texas Property Code Section 301.025, 'covered multifamily dwellings' -- buildings of four or more units that have an elevator, or ground-floor units in buildings without an elevator -- must be designed and constructed with certain accessibility features, including:
choice_a: Accessible common and public-use areas, doors wide enough for wheelchair passage, and usable kitchens and bathrooms allowing wheelchair maneuverability
choice_b: No accessibility features at all, since the requirement applies only to government-owned buildings
choice_c: Accessibility features only in buildings with fewer than four total units
choice_d: An elevator in every residential building regardless of height or unit count
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 301.025 imposes design-and-construction accessibility standards on covered multifamily dwellings, requiring accessible common areas, adequately wide doorways, accessible routes and controls, and usable kitchens/bathrooms -- a physical building-code-style requirement distinct from the reasonable-accommodation/modification duties owed to individual residents.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 301, Section 301.025 (design and construction requirements for covered multifamily dwellings), verified via texas.public.law

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Under Texas Property Code Section 301.025, when a tenant with a disability requests a reasonable modification to the physical premises (as distinct from a reasonable accommodation to a rule or policy), Texas law generally allows the landlord to require that:
choice_a: The modification be made at the requesting tenant's own expense
choice_b: The landlord pay for all such physical modifications out of pocket in every case
choice_c: No modification of any kind ever be permitted, regardless of disability
choice_d: The tenant permanently vacate the unit before any modification is discussed
explanation: A key distinction under fair housing law is that a reasonable accommodation (a change to a rule, policy, or service) is generally provided at no cost to the resident, while a reasonable modification (a physical change to the premises) may be required to be made and paid for by the requesting tenant, subject to reasonable conditions such as restoring the unit at move-out.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 301, Section 301.025 (reasonable modifications), verified via texas.public.law; National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.3-4

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Under Texas Property Code Section 301.081, an aggrieved person alleging a discriminatory housing practice under the Texas Fair Housing Act must file a written, sworn complaint with the commission no later than:
choice_a: The first anniversary of the date the alleged discriminatory housing practice occurred or terminated, whichever is later
choice_b: 30 days after the incident, with no exceptions permitted
choice_c: There is no filing deadline of any kind
choice_d: Ten years after the incident occurred
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 301.081 requires a written, sworn housing discrimination complaint to be filed within one year of the date the discriminatory practice occurred or terminated, after which the commission investigates and notifies the respondent within 20 days.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 301, Section 301.081 (complaint procedures), verified via texas.public.law

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: The Texas state agency division principally responsible for administering and enforcing the Texas Fair Housing Act (Texas Property Code Chapter 301) and processing state-level housing discrimination complaints is the:
choice_a: Texas Workforce Commission's Civil Rights Division
choice_d: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, exclusively
explanation: The Texas Workforce Commission's Civil Rights Division administers Texas Property Code Chapter 301 (the Texas Fair Housing Act) and investigates state-level housing discrimination complaints, operating as HUD's substantially-equivalent state agency partner rather than TREC, which regulates licensee conduct rather than fair housing enforcement generally.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 301 (Texas Fair Housing Act, administered by the commission); National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.6

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A lender's practice of refusing to make mortgage loans, or offering only less favorable loan terms, within certain geographic areas based on the racial or ethnic composition of the neighborhood -- rather than on the creditworthiness of individual applicants -- is known as:
explanation: Redlining is the illegal practice of denying or limiting financial services, particularly mortgage lending, to residents of specific geographic areas based on the racial or ethnic composition of those areas rather than individual creditworthiness -- distinct from steering, which involves directing individual buyers toward or away from neighborhoods.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.4 (illegal practices, enforcement, and penalties), Pearson VUE #094401

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: An agent who contacts homeowners in a stable, racially mixed neighborhood and urges them to sell quickly by suggesting property values will soon decline because members of a particular race are moving in is engaging in the illegal practice of:
explanation: Blockbusting (sometimes called panic peddling) is the illegal practice of inducing residential sales by suggesting a change in the racial or ethnic composition of a neighborhood will cause undesirable consequences, such as declining property values or increased crime -- profiting from manufactured fear rather than a legitimate market signal.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.4 (illegal practices, enforcement, and penalties), Pearson VUE #094401

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: In Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project (2015), the U.S. Supreme Court held that Fair Housing Act liability may be established through:
choice_a: Disparate impact theory -- a facially neutral policy that has a disproportionate discriminatory effect on a protected class, even without proof of discriminatory intent
choice_b: Only direct proof of intentional discrimination, with disparate impact claims barred entirely
choice_c: No theory at all, since the Court held the Fair Housing Act does not apply to state housing agencies
explanation: In this landmark Texas case, the Supreme Court confirmed that Fair Housing Act claims may proceed under a disparate impact theory -- liability for a facially neutral policy that disproportionately and unjustifiably harms a protected class -- in addition to traditional disparate treatment (intentional discrimination) claims.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C.4 (illegal practices and enforcement); Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Several competing brokerages secretly agree among themselves to refuse to show listings from, or cooperate with, a discount brokerage that charges lower commissions. This coordinated refusal to deal is known as a:
choice_a: Group boycott, a per se violation of federal antitrust law
choice_d: Permitted competitive response to a rival's pricing
explanation: A group boycott -- competitors agreeing to collectively refuse to deal with a targeted business or individual -- is a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, alongside price-fixing, market allocation, and certain tying arrangements, because it eliminates competition rather than responding to it individually.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.D.4 (antitrust laws), Pearson VUE #094401

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: Competing brokerages agree with each other to divide a metropolitan area into exclusive territories, with each firm agreeing not to solicit business in the others' assigned areas. This is an antitrust violation known as:
explanation: Market allocation is an agreement among competitors to divide up territories or types of customers rather than competing for all of them -- a per se Sherman Act violation, since it artificially eliminates competition within each firm's assigned market segment.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.D.4 (antitrust laws), Pearson VUE #094401

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A brokerage requires every buyer who uses its agents to also purchase title insurance from the brokerage's affiliated title company as a condition of receiving brokerage services. This practice raises concern as a potential antitrust:
choice_a: Tie-in (tying) arrangement, which may also implicate RESPA Section 8's prohibition on required use of affiliated settlement service providers
choice_d: A universally permitted bundling practice carrying no legal exposure
explanation: A tie-in (tying) arrangement conditions the sale of one product or service on the purchase of another, distinct, product or service; requiring clients to use an affiliated title company as a condition of brokerage representation can raise both antitrust tying concerns and a separate RESPA Section 8 required-use violation.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.D.4 (antitrust laws), Pearson VUE #094401

topic: Real Estate Practice, Fair Housing & Risk Management
question: A brokerage reduces its fair housing liability exposure by adopting a written office policy requiring every agent to offer identical services, information, and property showings to all prospective clients regardless of protected-class status. This practice is best described as a risk-management technique of:
choice_a: Consistent, uniform treatment and documentation of all client interactions
choice_b: Selective disclosure of listings based on client characteristics
choice_d: An unnecessary formality with no real liability benefit
explanation: Uniform treatment of all clients -- offering the same range of listings, information, and services regardless of a prospective client's protected-class status, and documenting that consistency -- is a core fair housing risk-management technique that helps a brokerage defend against discrimination claims and testing programs.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.D (risk management and reduction techniques), Pearson VUE #094401
